title: Exclusive | Third-oldest home in New York — visited by George Washington, King Philippe, and friendly ghosts — hits market for $8M
excerpt: A slice of really cool New York history is up for grabs.
content:
A slice of really cool New York history is up for grabs. 

Glen Sanders Mansion, the riverfront estate in Scotia, NY, believed to be the third-oldest surviving dwelling in New York State, has hit the market for $8 million, The Post has learned. 

The 75,000-square-foot property traces to 1658, when Scottish merchant Alexander Lindsay Glen built a stone dwelling on the Mohawk River and named the settlement Scotia, after his homeland. 

That one-room structure still stands, folded into the mansion around it, and the family held the estate 266 years until it was sold in 1962.

“That room is still part of the house, which would make it the third oldest,” listing agent Angelo Michael Mazzone Jr, son of the mansion’s current owner, confirmed to The Post. 

According to long-held family tradition, the property survived the 1690 Schenectady Massacre because the Glens had once shown kindness to French prisoners, and French officers reportedly crossed the river the next morning to breakfast at the family’s home.

The mansion standing today was built in 1713 by Alexander’s son — Captain Johannes “John” Glen — reportedly using stone, timber and doors salvaged from that original 1658 house.

Restaurateur Angelo Mazzone Sr bought the estate in 1988, opening it a year later as the flagship of what became Mazzone Hospitality. 

“We used to cater on their lawn. So when the house went up for sale, I said, well, we can make this a great restaurant and banquet hall,” Mazzone Sr said.

Now 75, he said the decision to sell comes down to age. 

“I’ve worked 40, 50 years struggling, working really hard to keep everything up and running,” he said. 

His son isn’t taking over: “I’m an opera singer and a real estate agent,” Mazzone Jr said. “I decided not to do this.”

Mazzone Hospitality, the operating company, was sold to Compass International five years ago, but Mazzone Sr remains sole owner of the real estate itself. 

“It was my baby. I grew a company from this facility to a $70 million food and beverage company,” he said. “But there’s really no one in my family that wanted to do it.”

The mansion’s calling card is its list of storied visitors. 

George Washington stopped there while surveying the region’s northern defenses in 1775, though historians have long noted he slept across the river at the John Glen House in Schenectady’s Stockade District. 

“It’s been verified that he was there for a tea party. Possibly stayed, but there’s no written documentation that he slept there,” Mazzone Jr said.

A young Louis Philippe, the future King of the French, is said to have stayed at the mansion during his American exile in the late 1790s, decades before he took the French throne in 1830, in a room still known as the Louis Philippe Bedroom. 

The historic dwelling maintains it’s original windows, floors, beams, staircase and the rock walls that hold up the beams, according to Mazzone Sr.

“All the original doors are here,” Mazzone Sr added. “So the doors that were put in in 1713, they’re all still working. But the doors that I put in, in 1989, I replaced 10 times.”

Family tradition holds that the mansion’s basement once sheltered freedom seekers as part of the Underground Railroad, with a passage said to connect the main house to a building across the street that later became the Scotia library. 

A visible mark on the original staircase banister is attributed to an Indigenous visitor, according to Mazzone Jr. 

“There’s actually a tomahawk mark in the banister from one of the Indians,” he said. 

Staff and family say the mansion has its share of unexplained activity, including a recurring sighting of a woman in a red dress some associate with Deborah Glen — the granddaughter of Alexander. 

 Mazzone Jr recalled an odd episode from when his father first bought the property.

“We pulled up, and every light was on in the house. So the three of us went in, turned off all the lights, and crossing the river, the whole house just lit up again.” 

A painter who worked alone in the mansion reported similar moments, he said, seeing “drapes moving and things like that she couldn’t explain.”

John Lawrence of Douglas Elliman who is co-listing the property alongside Mazzone and Rick Rosa said the family doesn’t dwell on the stories out of respect. 

“They’re friendly ghosts, and we don’t really like talking about them because they don’t want to be noticed.”

The listing includes roughly three acres, with the historic core measuring about 2,800 square feet inside the complex, which includes a 22-room inn. The mansion is not on the historical register, so there’s technically nothing stopping a buyer from tearing it down, though Mazzone Sr doubts the village would allow it, calling the house “really like the logo of the village.”

The sale also comes with a sweetener: entitlements for a previously approved 95-unit apartment complex with a ground-floor restaurant. 

Mazzone Sr had planned to develop it himself before changing course a month ago and deciding to sell instead. 

“If somebody was to purchase this and keep the historical house, it has been granted that we have some very strong entitlements that we would sell if somebody does want to develop and keep the original house,” Lawrence said.

For Mazzone Sr, the hope is simple. 

“I just hope they keep the old building. I just hope they preserve the old building the way we did. It’s really pretty incredible because the rooms are all exactly like they were.”
